blocks.text: Because God has deprived her of wisdom, nor has he imparted understanding to her] For although wisdom and understanding, if we wish to speak properly, belong only to human beings, who are endowed with reason, they are nevertheless also attributed to brute animals in Scripture. Thus the serpent is said to be the φρονιμώτατος [phronimōtatos] of all animals, Gen. III, 1. And Christ himself bids us imitate its prudence, Matth. X, 16. Isaiah too sets before us the example of the ox and the ass, which know their owner and their master's crib, Esa. I, 3. Jeremiah sets before us the stork, which knows her appointed times, and the turtledove, the crane and the swallow, which observe the time of their coming, Ierem. VIII, 7. And Solomon sets before us the ant, so that, having considered her ways, we may be wise, Prov. [II, 862] VI, 6. Indeed, although he was by far the wisest of men, he nevertheless praises four small creatures as חכמים מחכמים, exceedingly wise: namely, besides the ants, the choerogryllii, the locusts and the stellions, Prov. XXX, 24. But certain brute animals are said to be exceedingly wise: 1. Because they are as wise as is necessary for their own preservation. 2. Because they excel among the other brutes in this wisdom of theirs. Yet this wisdom falls short of human wisdom by many degrees, since it lacks the light of reason and is determined to a single end. But here God is said to have denied even this wisdom, such as it is, to the ostrich. He alone is the author not only of human ingenuity but also of that of the brutes. To this they refer what is found in Iob. XXXVIII, 36. according to the Chaldee and the Vulgate: Who gave the cock understanding? that is, no one other than God. Further, the Hebrew says of the ostrich כי השה אלוה חכמה, literally because God made her forget wisdom. For from נשה, to forget, the Hiphil is השה. But the Greeks have Κατεσιώπησεν αὐτῇ ὁ Θεὸς σοφίαν [Katesiōpēsen autē ho Theos sophian], God made wisdom silent for her. And the Syriac has ܐܣܓܝ, and the Arabic أكثر [akthara], he multiplied, in a sense not only different but entirely contrary. The Greeks, that is, read instead of השה, with He, חשה, with Cheth, he was silent or he made silent. And the Syriac, followed by the Arabic, inserting a Gimel, read השגה, he multiplied. But the Chaldee rightly has אנשיה, he made her forget wisdom. Now God is said to bring about forgetfulness of things past when a great change takes place: for instance, if prosperity follows adversity, or adversity prosperity. Thus Joseph, raised to the height of honours in Egypt, named his firstborn Manasseh, from forgetting. For God, he says, has made me forget my former toil, Gen. XLI, 51. Conversely, in the Babylonian captivity Jeremiah laments that God has caused the solemn feasts and sabbaths to be forgotten in Zion, Thren. II, 6. What is said here, that God made the ostrich forget wisdom, is not to be taken in that sense, as though she had previously remembered it and some change had occurred in her nature. For here to forget is nothing other than not to remember. This forgetfulness is not privative but negative, just as Moses calls the state before the creation of light darkness, not as a privation of light but as a mere negation, Gen. I, 3. Accordingly, in the following hemistich there is added ἐξηγητικῶς [exēgētikōs], ולא חלק לה בבינה, And he did not impart to her understanding, or prudence. Thus made her forget means did not impart. חלק, commonly to divide, here means to impart, like the Greek νέμειν [nemein]. Symmachus therefore rightly has Οὐκ ἔνειμεν αὐτῇ σύνεσιν [Ouk eneimen autē synesin], where the Elders have Οὐκ ἐπεμέρισεν αὐτῇ ἐν τῇ συνέσει [Ouk epemerisen autē en tē synesei], He did not distribute to her, or He did not give her a share in understanding. As it is said to Simon Magus in Actor. VIII, 21. Οὐκ ἔστι σοι μερὶς, οὐδὲ κλῆρος ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ· [Ouk esti soi meris, oude klēros en tō logō toutō] You have neither part [col. 257] nor lot in this matter; Act. VIII, 21.

There are some who hold that part of the eggs is neglected by the ostrich neither through imprudence nor through carelessness or ἀστοργίαν [astorgian], but by deliberate design, and that she does this [II, 863] with discrimination, rejecting only τὰ ὑπηνέμια [ta hypēnemia], or those which must be kept for feeding the chicks. Aelian, History, book 4, chapter 37: Ἡ στρουθὸς ἡ μεγάλη ὠὰ μὲν ἀποτίκτει πολλὰ, οὐ πάντα δὲ ἀποκύει, ἀλλ᾽ ἀποκρίνει τὰ ἄγονα, τοῖς δὲ ἐγκάρποις ἐπῳάζει, καὶ ἐκ μὲν τούτων τοὺς νεοττοὺς ἐξέλεψεν, ἐκεῖνα δὲ τὰ ἐκφαυλισθέντα τούτοις τροφὴν παρατίθησιν. [Hē strouthos hē megalē ōa men apotiktei polla, ou panta de apokyei, alla apokrinei ta agona, tois de enkarpois epōazei, kai ek men toutōn tous neottous exelepsen, ekeina de ta ekphaulisthenta toutois trophēn paratithēsin.] Although the ostrich lays many eggs, she does not use all of them for hatching, but sets apart the sterile ones and broods only on the fertile ones. When she has hatched the chicks from these, she sets the spoiled eggs before them as food. And Philes, in the place cited above:

Ὠῶν δὲ συχνῶν εὑρεθεῖσαν ἐργάτιν Τὰ μὴ καθαρά γε τῆς γονῆς ἀποκρίνειν· Ὅσους γὰρ ἐξέλεψεν ἡ ζέσις τόκους, Ἐν τοῖς ἀποῤῥεύσασι κυλίνδροις τρέφειν. [Ōōn de sychnōn heuretheisan ergatin / Ta mē kathara ge tēs gonēs apokrinein· / Hosous gar exelepsen hē zesis tokous, / En tois aporrheusasi kylindrois trephein.]
